summary:
Qatar criminalises consensual same-sex relations. Article 296 of the Penal Code (Law 11/2004) punishes sodomy with one to three years' imprisonment, and the prohibition applies to Muslims and non-Muslims alike; sexual acts between men and between women are both covered. For Muslims convicted in sharia courts a capital sentence remains a theoretical possibility, though it has never been imposed. Article 296 replaced Article 201 of the 1971 Penal Code, which had carried up to five years, and before that Article 171 of the 1956 code, with the colonial-era Indian Penal Code imposed through Order in Council in 1938. The sources record no statute repealing or legalising this exposure.

Trans people face a distinct detention power: they may be held for up to six months without trial or charge on suspicion of "impersonating the opposite gender" or of violating "public morality" and "community protection" provisions. Human Rights Watch reported on 24 October 2022 that Qatar's security forces arrested and abused LGBT people between 2019 and 2022, documenting six cases of severe repeated beatings and five cases of sexual harassment in police custody. Arrests took place in public places on the sole basis of gender expression and were accompanied by unlawful searches. Mistreatment was recorded as recently as September 2022, during the period when Qatar was preparing to host the 2022 World Cup under international scrutiny.

Abuse by police and other authorities against LGBT people has included beatings, torture and forced "conversion therapy". A May 2022 account by Naser Mohamed, the first Qatari to publicly come out as gay, described LGBT people being held and physically abused, then promised safety from further torture if they agreed to become informants against others. BBC-sourced information states that trans detainees are required to undergo forced physical detransition, including surgical removal of breast tissue, while held, and must attend conversion "therapy" on release; Qatari authorities "categorically rejected" those allegations.

Detentions have targeted visitors as well as residents. On 4 February 2024 a dual British-Mexican citizen was arrested after police ran a fake Grindr profile; he was held 44 days, interrogated about other gay men, forced to sign documents in Arabic without a translator and denied a lawyer. The UN Working Group on Arbitrary Detention raised concerns about his treatment, and detainees in that case were denied access to antiretroviral medicines needed to live with HIV, a denial the Working Group also flagged. In 2016 the Polish Instagram star King Luxy spent two months in custody on suspicion of being homosexual. In 1998 an American visitor was sentenced to six months in prison and 90 lashes for homosexual activity.

In May 2023 Gilbert Ignatius, a Qatar Airways employee, was detained by Qatar's Criminal Investigation Department over his appearance, with tinted moisturizer, designer clothing and a bag cited as evidence of prostitution; an officer told him "You have no rights. This is Qatar," and struck him when he asked to contact the Indonesian embassy. He was later deported, fired and banned from Qatar without official explanation. Ignatius reported that post-World Cup secret police crackdowns especially target people who appear to be from the Philippines, Indonesia and Thailand.

The government does not recognise same-sex marriage, civil unions or domestic partnerships, and cohabitation is itself illegal. Because same-gender couples cannot marry, the local death penalty for same-gender sex is argued to apply only to Muslims through extramarital-sex provisions.

Entry and public conduct are framed by official statements rather than by a written visitor rule. In May 2022 the Emir Sheikh Tamim bin Hamad Al Thani said LGBTQ visitors would be welcomed to the World Cup but must respect the nation's culture, and in 2013 bid chief Hassan Al-Thawadi said all were welcome provided they refrained from public displays of affection. In May 2022 some hotels on FIFA's official recommended accommodation list refused to serve same-sex couples outright, while others accepted them only if they hid their relationship in public; FIFA said it would remind hotels of non-discrimination requirements. Nasser Al Khater said in December 2021 that public display of affection "is frowned upon", and Major General al-Ansari warned that rainbow flags could be confiscated to "protect" fans. In 2013 Kuwait proposed banning gay foreigners from entering any Gulf Cooperation Council country and the GCC agreed to discuss it, then backtracked, possibly over concerns about the effect on Qatar's 2022 World Cup hosting.
tangentialFactors:
Cultural norms in Qatar view homosexuality and cross-dressing harshly, and the sources describe a strong social taboo around the subject: a 2016 Doha News opinion piece by a gay Qatari man writing as "Majid Al-Qatari" drew extremely strong reactions for allowing the topic to be discussed, and PinkNews reported on 20 July 2018 that the piece was called "jarring" and attributed "irreparable damage to mental health" to its subject.

Official hostility is also expressed through information control. In 2018 nine articles on gay and transgender rights were censored from the Doha edition of The New York Times International Edition, prompting the Government Communications Office to pledge an investigation. Qatar voted against the UN independent expert on sexual orientation and gender identity at the Human Rights Council in 2016, 2019, 2022 and 2025. In June 2019 the state-linked outlet AJ+ marked LGBTQ Pride Month, prompting criticism of the paradox with domestic censorship, and in 2022 Transport for London banned Qatari advertising after Qatar moved to block rainbow armbands, with Qatar subsequently reviewing its London investments.

The Australian men's national team publicly called in October 2022 for Qatar to recognise same-sex marriage, an example of external pressure on the framework that has not produced a legal change. The legal history runs the other way in severity: the 1971 code's predecessor provisions and the 1956 code carried longer maximum sentences than Article 296 does today, so the current framework is not the harshest version Qatar has had on the books.
localsOnly:
The government does not allow people in Qatar to campaign for LGBTQ rights, and in 2022 police arrested protesters who criticised Qatari law. Residents who are found to have organised or publicly advocated on the issue face the same detention powers described for visitors.

Employment and residence status are direct levers. Gilbert Ignatius was deported, dismissed from his job and banned from Qatar without official explanation after his May 2023 detention, and he reported that post-World Cup secret police crackdowns especially target people who appear to be from the Philippines, Indonesia and Thailand. In the 1990s the Philippine Overseas Employment Administration told Philippine workers that gay workers were prohibited in Qatar after mass arrests and deportations.

For people already in custody the consequences are procedural as well as physical: detainees have been pressured to become informants against others in exchange for safety from torture, and BBC-sourced reporting describes mandatory surgical detransition during detention plus compulsory conversion "therapy" on release, allegations Qatari authorities reject. Cohabitation between same-gender partners is itself illegal, so shared residence can be a charge in its own right.
outOfScopeNotes:
No source in the inventory addresses legal gender recognition, identity-document markers for trans people, or whether a trans visitor's passport gender affects entry screening. That gap is unresolved here, not answered by the sources.

Whether Article 296 has been applied to women in practice, and how often it is enforced against residents rather than visitors, is not sourced. The inventory supplies individual cases and a 2019-2022 pattern of arrests but no prosecution statistics.

The claim that the sharia capital penalty applies to same-sex conduct is described in the sources as theoretical and never imposed; the argument that it reaches only Muslims through extramarital-sex provisions is presented as a legal reading rather than a settled holding, and no court decision resolving it is cited.

Qatari authorities "categorically rejected" the BBC-sourced allegations of forced surgical detransition and mandatory conversion therapy. The denial stands alongside the reporting and neither side is independently corroborated in this inventory.

The enforcement status of the hotel non-discrimination requirements FIFA said it would raise, and whether the 2013 Gulf Cooperation Council entry-ban proposal was ever adopted in any form, are unresolved: the sources record the proposal, the discussion and the backtrack only.

No source states whether hate-crime enhancements, anti-discrimination law, or partner/next-of-kin recognition of any kind exist in Qatar beyond the finding that marriage, civil unions and domestic partnerships are not recognised.
